newsitem.title: SPAIN: INTERVIEW - Latam bank margins to retain lure-BBV.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Latam bank margins to retain lure-BBV.

text.p: Spanish banks in Latin America are likely to enjoy the region's ample margins well into the next century before hefty competition reduces them to European levels, a top official at Banco Bilbao Vizcaya said on Tuesday.
"We could have some 15 years before the margins fall to really tough levels," Ignacio Sanchez-Asiain Sanz, BBV sub-director general, said in an interview.
He put the traditional banking margin between interest rates on lending and borrowing at an average seven to eight percent in Latin America, more than triple the Spanish average.
"The margins (in Latin America) are substantial. They are declining but not rapidly," said Sanchez-Asiain, who oversees Latin American holdings for the group.
"In periods of high growth, margins don't typically decline substantially because one doesn't get into fierce competition. There is room for everybody."

Top Spanish banks have been pouring funds into Latin America. They are eager to capitalise on the high growth and margins to compensate for falling domestic margins and for the potential loss of business tied to the launch of the euro set for 1999.

"Our strategy is to be a universal bank and we believe that this only makes sense and will only be profitable if one has a position of leadership....When the market matures if we are not among the banks of reference we will never be profitable," Sanchez-Asiain said.

This year, after an aggressive 1996 shopping spree, BBV has acquired 40 percent of Provincial in Venezuela and 71.7 percent of Credito Argentino. As of May, BBV had assets of 3.9 trillion pesetas ($26.7 billion) and 1,150 offices in Latin America.

BBV expects to benefit from what is likely to be explosive growth in retail banking as the economic recovery spurs middle class growth and the balance of bank profits shifts away from heavy reliance on corporate business.

"In general, what we see in Latin America overall and not just at banks BBV owns, is that the majority of profits come from dealings with corporations and I think this is going to change bit by bit as new middle classes are created. That is why we all invested," Sanchez-Asiain said.
The objectives for its Latin American business are steep.

BBV expects a return on equity of at least 20 percent, well above the 14 percent threshold it sets in the less risky Spanish market. In the near future, it wants foreign business to represent 25 percent of its profits, he said.
But the business opportunities justify them, he said.
In the first quarter, BBV's Latin American units provided pre-tax profits of 10.45 billion pesetas, compared with total pre-tax group profit of 57.77 billion.
But in addition to rapid growth in retail banking, BBV is setting its sights on expanding private international banking and in capitalising on its capital market expertise.
Medium-term the group seeks growing business with multinationals, particularly those from North America, attracted by its presence in various markets.
